implementation_notes: Hibernate implements the Jakarta Persistence TABLE_PER_CLASS strategy: annotate the abstract base entity with @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.TABLE_PER_CLASS) and every concrete entity maps to its own table containing all of its columns, inherited ones included; no discriminator column is needed. Polymorphic queries over the base type are executed as a UNION over the concrete tables, and because keys must be unique across the hierarchy an IDENTITY generator cannot be used - use a shared SEQUENCE or TABLE generator. Note that support for this strategy is optional in the Jakarta Persistence specification, so it is a Hibernate capability you should not assume on another provider.
pitfalls: GenerationType.IDENTITY fails with TABLE_PER_CLASS because each table would mint its own keys; use SEQUENCE/TABLE (or UUID) so keys stay unique across the hierarchy.
Polymorphic queries compile to a union: every subclass branch must select the same column count with NULL padding, which Hibernate generates but the database cannot index as a whole.
TABLE_PER_CLASS support is optional in Jakarta Persistence, so code that must be portable across providers cannot rely on it.

variants.name: Hand-written JDBC DAO per concrete table
variants.idiom_name: one DAO plus row mapper per concrete class over PreparedStatement
variants.implementation_notes: Without an ORM the hierarchy disappears from the mapping layer: write one DAO (or one MyBatis mapper) per concrete class that reads and writes exactly its own table through PreparedStatement, with the inherited columns as ordinary fields. Mixed collections are a hand-written UNION ALL with NULL padding and a type tag, or several DAO calls merged in the service layer. This is the route when the team wants explicit SQL and full control of the denormalized schema, and it is the only route on providers that do not implement TABLE_PER_CLASS.
pitfalls: Hand-written DAOs are where the duplicated base columns drift: a shared column must be changed in every DAO, row mapper and migration.
A UNION ALL across the concrete tables must pad each branch with NULLs and keep JDBC types consistent, or the result-set mapping breaks at runtime.
Per-table identity keys collide: use one sequence, a UUID, or a shared key table before reading the tables as one hierarchy.
